title: Promoting Science, Technology, and Engineering Self-Efficacy and Knowledge for All With an Autism Inclusion Maker Program
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an inclusive maker program, IDEAS (Inventing, Designing, and Engineering for All Students), can improve STEM-related outcomes for middle school students in autism-inclusion settings. The authors ask whether participation in the program increases students’ STEM self-efficacy, career interest, and understanding/engagement with the engineering design process (EDP), and whether effects differ for autistic students versus their general education peers.

IDEAS was adapted from a museum-based maker curriculum and delivered as an afterschool or lunchtime club in three public middle schools in New York City. The intervention was designed collaboratively by maker educators, autism inclusion specialists, engineers, researchers, and school staff, and included supports such as checklists, visual templates, and explicit prompts. Students in grades 6–8 participated voluntarily; treatment students joined the maker club while comparison students did not. The study combined hierarchical linear modeling of pre/post survey and EDP assessment data with observations and interviews.

The quantitative findings showed positive effects for the maker group overall on technology and engineering self-efficacy, technology and engineering interest, vicarious experience, science appreciation, and EDP understanding. However, the program’s effects on technology/engineering interest and science appreciation were stronger for neurotypical students than for autistic students. Qualitative findings suggested that the program supported repeated use of the EDP, enabled students to complete personally meaningful projects, and gave autistic students opportunities to demonstrate capability and socialize around shared interests. The paper concludes that interest-driven, well-supported maker programming can benefit diverse middle school learners in inclusive settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, baseline adjustment, and hierarchical linear modeling. It is not randomized and includes some concerns about self-selection into the maker program, so it does not meet blue-tier criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports medium-to-large positive effects on a priority population, including g=0.82 for self-efficacy and g=0.56 for engineering design process understanding. Even though the intervention is not Khanmigo and is not a science-achievement test, the observed impacts are substantively meaningful on relevant STEM learning and engagement outcomes.

interventions.use_case: inclusive interest-driven maker program for middle school students with autism inclusion, centered on engineering design activities such as paper circuits, 3D design/fabrication, and iterative prototyping

finding.finding_summary: The maker program improved students' understanding of the engineering design process (EDP) relative to the business-as-usual comparison group. The adjusted Hedges' g was 0.56, based on n=109 total participants (54 makers, 55 non-makers), with the EDP assessment measured via brief audio-recorded interviews coded on a 3-point scale.
finding.measure: Engineering Design Process (EDP) assessment; audio-recorded interview responses scored on a 3-point rubric

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced positive gains in technology and engineering self-efficacy compared with the comparison group, with Hedges' g=0.82. The study also found improvement in vicarious experience (g=0.60) and science appreciation (g=0.20), indicating increased confidence and interest in STEM-related engagement among makers (n=109).
finding.measure: STEM self-efficacy survey constructs: technology and engineering self-efficacy, vicarious experience of science, and science appreciation

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative findings suggest improved collaboration, persistence, and problem solving during maker activities, but these were not measured with a standardized durable-skills instrument. Students repeatedly iterated on designs, used peers as resources, and persisted through failures; however, these outcomes are descriptive rather than rigorously estimated effects.
finding.measure: Observations and teacher/student interviews focused on collaboration, iteration, persistence, and problem solving
